headline: SW Ledge slack at 11:40: stripers still biting the last of the ebb, bonito flashing off Sandy Point
subhead: The ledge is still producing on the right tide window, and the first bonito of the season are finally showing color off Block Island's southwest corner.
body_markdown:
_AI fishing-intelligence report. It was prepared from 0 supplied evidence records and 17 supplied analysis inputs; it does not claim firsthand fishing._

Slack at SW Ledge runs 11:40 this week, and the ninety minutes on either side of it are still the difference between a rod-bending drift and a long ride home with nothing to show for it. That's not a new rule — it's the oldest rule on this ledge — but with August heat pressing down on the surface layer, that tide window has gotten tighter and less forgiving. Miss it by twenty minutes and the current goes soft and mushy over the rockpile, and the bass that were stacked on the up-current side scatter into water too deep to reach with anything but a wire-line troll.

Striped bass are still there, though, and that's worth saying plainly because a lot of the surf reports coming out of the rest of the region this week describe fish pushed deep and lockjawed by warm water. SW Ledge in the 25-to-40-foot band is holding better than that. The pattern that's working is a heavy bucktail — 2 to 3 ounces depending on how hard the current is running — bounced tight to the rock structure on the last hour of the ebb, then switched to a slow, deliberate swim through the first hour of the flood as the current reverses and bait gets disoriented over the ledge. Eels fished on a fish-finder rig, drifted right along that same current seam, have been the better bet for anything over 20 pounds. Nothing here is a guaranteed 35-pounder every trip — the bite has been more about putting time into the right ninety minutes than blind luck — but the fish are present and eating when the tide sets up.

Block Island is where the real story is developing. We flagged it a few days back — said the bonito threshold was close and arrivals were imminent — and the first flashes are showing now off the southwest side, working the rip line that runs off Sandy Point down toward the deeper water. They're not thick yet. This is early-arrival behavior: small pods showing on the surface for a few minutes at a time, usually right at the top of the tide change when bait gets pinned against the rip. Small metal — half-ounce Deadly Dicks or similar — cast ahead of a breaking pod and retrieved fast has drawn strikes, but the window on any given pod has been short. Patience and moving water are doing more work right now than any specific lure choice.

False albacore are mixed in with some of those bonito sightings but haven't separated out into their own dedicated run yet. That's normal for early August — the albie show off Block usually needs another week or two of consistent warm water before it becomes its own event rather than a byproduct of the bonito arrival. Worth watching Clay Head and the rip off North Light as the week develops; that's typically where the albies show first once the run gets legs, usually a little later in the month than the bonito.

Bluefish have been the most reliable violence of the week. Wherever bunker pods have held tight — and they've been holding tight along the beach fronts and off the breakwater at Galilee — the blitzes have been real: surface explosions, birds working low, blues in the 4-to-8-pound class crashing bait hard enough to see from a hundred yards out. That's exactly the pattern we called — stable high pressure holding the bunker schools together, and the blues cashing in on it. Topwater poppers or a simple bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig both work once you're in the middle of it; the trick is getting there while the pod is still tight, because these blitzes don't sit still.

Fluke fishing has stayed steady rather than spectacular in the deeper water southwest of Block Island, 50 to 70 feet, drifting white and chartreuse Gulp paired with a bucktail teaser. Keeper-class fish are coming, along with a healthy number of shorts that need throwing back, which tells you the size structure out there is still building toward better numbers later in the month. Black sea bass on the rocky humps in that same depth range have been a dependable consolation prize on days when the fluke bite goes quiet — squid strips or Gulp on a double-hook rig, bounced slow along bottom.

Looking ahead, the tide windows at SW Ledge tighten again as the week progresses, and I'd plan trips around that 11:40 slack shifting later each day rather than fighting the current when it's running hard and directionless. If the bonito pods off Sandy Point keep building the way the early signs suggest, expect more consistent surface action by the middle of next week rather than the scattered showing happening now. That's the bet I'd make with a trip this weekend — fish the ledge on the tide, then run out to the rip off Block Island and see what's showing on top.
